canonical_statement: The activity reviews the anatomy, microbiology, evaluation, treatment, prevention, and interprofessional management of odontogenic and orofacial infections.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This activity reviews the anatomy, microbiology, evaluation, treatment, prevention, and optimization of managing infections secondary to odontogenic and orofacial sources.

canonical_statement: Odontogenic infections are among the most common infections worldwide.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Infections of dental origin—odontogenic infections—are among the most common infections worldwide.

canonical_statement: In adults, odontogenic infections are described as the primary cause of deep neck infections.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: in adults, odontogenic infections are the primary cause of deep neck infections.

canonical_statement: Maxillary canine infection can extend from the tooth root into the canine space.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Infection of a maxillary canine can extend from the tooth root into the canine space.

canonical_statement: A maxillary molar root that extends superior to the buccinator insertion can permit spread into facial subcutaneous tissues.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A maxillary molar root extending superiorly to the insertion can allow for the spread of infection into the subcutaneous tissues of the face.

canonical_statement: Mandibular dental infections can involve the sublingual, submandibular, and submental spaces.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Infections of the mandibular teeth can lead to infections in three different spaces.

canonical_statement: The free posterior border of the mylohyoid allows infection to spread readily between the submandibular and sublingual spaces.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The posterior border of the mylohyoid is free, allowing infection to spread between the submandibular and sublingual spaces easily.

canonical_statement: For mandibular infections, tooth-root position relative to the mylohyoid line largely determines whether medial spread reaches the sublingual or submandibular space.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The spread of odontogenic infections of mandibular origin is largely based on the position of the tooth roots relative to the mylohyoid line.

canonical_statement: Direct spread to the submental space from a tooth root is uncommon; spread often occurs from adjacent submandibular or sublingual spaces.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Spread to the submental space is unlikely to occur directly from the tooth root and often occurs due to spread from the submandibular space, sublingual space, or directly from the skin.

canonical_statement: Oral flora are dominated by bacteria, especially anaerobes and facultative anaerobes.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The flora of the oral cavity is diverse, but it is dominated by bacteria, particularly anaerobes and facultative anaerobes.

canonical_statement: The source states that more than 700 bacterial types, along with fungi, inhabit the oral cavity.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: It is estimated that over 700 types of bacteria live within the oral cavity and various types of fungi.

canonical_statement: Streptococcus is described as the most common bacterial genus in the oral cavity.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The most common bacterial genus by far is Streptococcus

canonical_statement: Odontogenic infections are described as nearly always polymicrobial, supporting broad empiric antimicrobial coverage.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: nearly all odontogenic infections are polymicrobial; treatment is therefore broadly directed even after culture results.

canonical_statement: Odontogenic infections can spread rapidly and threaten neurovascular structures and airway patency.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: odontogenic infections can quickly spread and compromise neurovascular structures and airway patency.

canonical_statement: Dental caries are described as the leading cause of odontogenic infection, with periapical abscess the most common infection type.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Dental caries is the leading cause of odontogenic infection, the most common of which is the periapical abscess.

canonical_statement: Management commonly combines antibiotics with drainage or debridement; the source calls definitive dental extraction the gold standard, with endodontic preservation possible in selected cases.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Treatment often involves a combination of enteral or intravenous antibiotics and surgical drainage or debridement. In any case of odontogenic or orofacial infection, treatment by definitive dental extraction is the gold standard

canonical_statement: The source reports that by age 65 more than 90% of people in the United States will have experienced dental caries.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: by age 65, over 90% of people will have experienced dental caries.

canonical_statement: The source reports that men are more commonly affected and that more than 70% of odontogenic infections occur in patients aged 20 to 50 years.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Men are more commonly affected than women, and over 70% of infections occur in patients between 20 and 50 years old.

canonical_statement: Tobacco use and diabetes are described as the comorbid conditions most commonly associated with odontogenic neck infections.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Tobacco use and diabetes are the most commonly associated comorbid conditions with odontogenic neck infections.

canonical_statement: The review states that odontogenic infection is currently the leading cause of deep neck infection in U.S. adults.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: currently the leading cause of deep neck infection in adults in the United States.

canonical_statement: Patients classically have one to two weeks of worsening dental pain before facial or neck swelling.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Patients with odontogenic infections classically present with one to two weeks of worsening dental pain preceding facial or neck swelling.

canonical_statement: Common symptoms include odynophagia, neck or facial pain, trismus, fever, and malaise.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A review of systems commonly reveals odynophagia, neck pain, facial pain, trismus, fever, and malaise.

canonical_statement: Depending on the source tooth and direction of spread, patients may report paresthesias, ocular pain, diplopia, dyspnea, or sialorrhea.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Depending on the tooth of origin and direction of spread, these patients can report paresthesias, ocular pain, diplopia, dyspnea, and sialorrhea.

canonical_statement: Intraoral rupture of an abscess can produce foul-tasting and foul-smelling purulent secretions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Patients who have had a rupture of the abscess intraorally may complain of foul tasting and smelling secretions as a result of pus in the oral cavity.

canonical_statement: Early odontogenic cellulitis can often be evaluated clinically and treated as an outpatient.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: a physical exam for evaluation.

canonical_statement: Findings consistent with cellulitis include erythema, edema, induration, tenderness, and acute tender cervical lymphadenopathy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Skin and mucosal findings consistent with cellulitis include erythema, edema, induration, tenderness, and acute, tender cervical lymphadenopathy.

canonical_statement: Point-of-care ultrasound can be used to evaluate suspected abscess formation.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Point of care ultrasound (POCUS) can be used to evaluate for abscess formation if there is a concern.

canonical_statement: If POCUS is unreliable because of bone shadowing or body habitus, CT with intravenous contrast can help distinguish cellulitis from abscess.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A computed tomography (CT) scan is unnecessary but can be a useful adjunct in patients in whom bone shadow or body habitus makes POCUS an unreliable imaging modality. In this case, a CT scan with intravenous contrast can aid in differentiating cellulitis from an abscess.

canonical_statement: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and face should be considered when a complex abscess or deep-neck-space spread is suspected.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A contrasted CT scan of the neck and face should be considered in cases where concern for complex abscess formation or spread to deep neck spaces is suspected.

canonical_statement: Prominent neck or oral swelling with stridor, dyspnea, or frank respiratory distress requires rapid upper-airway evaluation in a controlled setting, preferably with awake flexible laryngoscopy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In cases of prominent neck and oral cavity swelling, stridor, dyspnea, and frank respiratory distress, rapid evaluation of the upper airway must be performed in a controlled setting. This is best done by awake flexible laryngoscopy

canonical_statement: For odontogenic cellulitis, the source recommends broad-spectrum therapy and lists amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin for penicillin-allergic patients as commonly effective options.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: commonly, these infections are effectively treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin in penicillin-allergic patients.

canonical_statement: Timely extraction of the infected tooth is described as a means of eliminating the infectious nidus and halting progression.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Timely dental extraction by a dentist can expedite treatment and halt progression as the necrotic tooth serves as the infectious nidus.

canonical_statement: Delayed cellulitis can progress to suppuration and abscess formation.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: If treatment is delayed, cellulitis can progress to suppuration and abscess formation.

canonical_statement: Fluctuance, significant mass effect, and suppurative dental sockets are findings that favor abscess over cellulitis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Physical exam findings more suggestive of an abscess include fluctuance, significant mass effect, and suppurative dental sockets.

canonical_statement: Most minor odontogenic abscesses can be identified with POCUS and do not require CT.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Most minor abscesses do not require a CT scan and can be identified with POCUS

canonical_statement: Drainage of an odontogenic abscess is recommended for source control and palliation.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Drainage of an abscess is recommended both for source control and palliation.

canonical_statement: When feasible, transoral drainage is preferred because it has the least morbidity and conceals incisions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: transoral drainage confers the least morbidity and effectively conceals incisions; it should be attempted whenever feasible.

canonical_statement: Needle aspiration, incision and drainage, and temporary drains may be combined according to abscess size, location, and patient factors.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Needle aspiration, incision and drainage, and temporary drain placement can be used in combination depending on the size, location, and patient.

canonical_statement: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration can confirm the abscess cavity location before formal incision and drainage.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: ultrasound-guided needle aspiration can be used to confirm the location of the abscess cavity before formal incision and drainage are attempted

canonical_statement: For abscess, extraction of the offending tooth together with antimicrobial therapy is indicated.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: As with cellulitis, extraction of the offending tooth coupled with antibiosis is indicated.

canonical_statement: Although abscess culture is recommended, the review states that culture results rarely change management because these infections are polymicrobial.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A culture swab of the abscess cavity should be taken, although due to the aforementioned polymicrobial nature of these infections, it rarely affects management.

canonical_statement: Many odontogenic abscesses can be managed as outpatients with oral antibiotics, whereas extensive infection, immunodeficiency, or significant comorbidity favors intravenous antibiotics and inpatient monitoring.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Many patients with odontogenic abscesses can be treated as an outpatient with oral antibiotics, but those with more extensive infections, immunodeficiency, or comorbid medical conditions should be given intravenous antibiotics and resuscitated and monitored as an inpatient.

canonical_statement: Ludwig angina is described as a rapidly spreading phlegmonous infection of the bilateral submandibular, submental, and sublingual spaces, usually presenting as cellulitis before suppuration.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: rapid and phlegmonous infection of bilateral submandibular, submental, and sublingual spaces.

canonical_statement: Ludwig angina is an airway emergency because edema of the floor-of-mouth spaces and tongue can critically narrow the upper airway.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Ludwig angina is an emergency given the mass effect of the infection on the upper airway. The infection promotes edema of the six spaces as well as the tongue

canonical_statement: Classic Ludwig angina features include respiratory distress, drooling, and a bullfrog appearance of the anterior neck.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A classic clinical appearance of the patient with Ludwig’s angina is respiratory distress, drooling, and a “bullfrog” appearance of the anterior neck.

canonical_statement: Management of Ludwig angina should prioritize airway stabilization; after airway control, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and inpatient admission are warranted, with surgery when needed.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Management should prioritize airway assessment and stability with the simultaneous implementation of both short- and long-term airway stabilizing strategies. After securing the airway, these patients warrant prompt, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and inpatient admission.

canonical_statement: The source reports that odontogenic disease accounts for nearly 40% of acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Sinusitis of odontogenic origin is common, accounting for nearly 40% of all acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis.

canonical_statement: Maxillary molars and premolars are closely associated with the maxillary sinus, and dental implants or persistent oroantral fistulas can serve as routes for infection.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The maxillary teeth, particularly the molars and pre-molars, are closely associated with the maxillary sinus.

canonical_statement: Unilateral isolated maxillary sinusitis on imaging favors an odontogenic source compared with typical non-odontogenic rhinosinusitis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Imaging often shows unilateral isolated maxillary sinusitis, whereas non-odontogenic rhinosinusitis is often bilateral and involves other sinuses.

canonical_statement: Management of odontogenic sinusitis may require dental or implant extraction, antibiotics, and endoscopic sinus surgery.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Treatment consists similarly of dental or implant extraction, antibiosis, and possible surgical intervention of the sinuses (endoscopic sinus surgery).

canonical_statement: For odontogenic sinusitis from a persistent oroantral fistula, the review recommends fistula repair after infection resolution.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Patients with odontogenic sinusitis resulting from persistent oroantral fistula benefit most from repair of the fistula following resolution of the infection.

canonical_statement: Repeated odontogenic-appearing infections in an otherwise healthy patient can signal oral cavity malignancy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: repeated infections or infection in an otherwise healthy individual can be an indicator of oral cavity malignancy.

canonical_statement: Follow-up should confirm resolution of mucosal or bony irregularities and maintain a low threshold for biopsy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Dental or surgical follow-up should assess for resolution of any mucosal or bony irregularities and maintain a low threshold for biopsy.

canonical_statement: When no clearly infected tooth is present or the dental-pain history is doubtful, nearby anatomy should be investigated clinically and with imaging when appropriate.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: investigation of the nearby anatomy should be performed through a physical exam or imaging studies when applicable.

canonical_statement: Patients with odontogenic infection among multiple soft-tissue infections should be evaluated for congenital or acquired immunodeficiency.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Patients presenting with odontogenic infections as one of many soft tissue infections should be evaluated for possible immunodeficiencies, either congenital or acquired.

canonical_statement: The review summarizes a 200-patient emergency-department cohort in which more than half were discharged the same day, fewer than half were admitted, and about half of admitted patients underwent surgery.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In a 2022 study of 200 patients who presented to the emergency department with odontogenic infections, over half were discharged same-day with medical therapy. Less than half necessitated inpatient admission, and approximately 50% of those admitted necessitated surgical intervention.

canonical_statement: In the same secondary-reported cohort, the review states that there was one morbidity event and two necrotizing soft-tissue infections requiring multiple debridements.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Of the entire cohort, there was only one morbidity and two patients with necrotizing soft tissue infections requiring multiple debridements.

canonical_statement: Deep-space infection can spread from masticator or submandibular spaces into parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal, carotid, and prevertebral spaces; prevertebral spread can reach the mediastinum and chest.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: These spaces have open boundaries with other deep neck spaces allowing for direct spread to the parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal, and carotid spaces of the neck. The prevertebral space, if infected, provides a rapid conduit into the mediastinum and chest

canonical_statement: Delayed treatment, poor nutrition, poor oral hygiene, and tobacco use can promote chronic osteomyelitis of the jaw.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: delayed treatment, poor nutrition, poor oral hygiene, and tobacco use can promote the development of chronic osteomyelitis.

canonical_statement: CT can identify sequestration, osteolysis, and necrosis in osteomyelitis; treatment consists of long-term culture-directed antibiotics and debridement of necrotic bone.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: CT scan can identify sequestration of infected bone, osteolysis, and areas of frank necrosis. Treatment consists of long-term culture-directed antibiotic therapy with debridement of necrotic bone.

canonical_statement: Airway compromise is described as the most common emergent sequela of odontogenic infection.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The most common emergent sequela of odontogenic infections is airway compromise

canonical_statement: Intravenous antibiotics and corticosteroids may reduce airway edema but require time to work; racemic epinephrine may reduce tongue or oropharyngeal edema but cannot relieve abscess mass effect or deep-tissue edema.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Intravenous administration of antibiotics and corticosteroids can improve airway edema and obstruction, but these medications require significant time to take effect.

canonical_statement: Awake flexible laryngoscopy is often required because oral and neck examinations alone may incompletely define the level and nature of airway obstruction.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: An oral exam and neck exam can aid in evaluation, but often the exam is incomplete without an awake flexible laryngoscopy.

canonical_statement: Nasopharyngeal or, in obtunded patients, oropharyngeal airways can temporize tongue-base obstruction, but may not relieve parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal obstruction.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: placement of a nasopharyngeal airway or (in the obtunded patient) an oropharyngeal airway can alleviate tongue base obstruction. Obstruction secondary to parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spread may not be effectively treated by these methods.

canonical_statement: Severe obstructive disease may preclude direct or video laryngoscopy; the review describes awake fiberoptic intubation as effective when the glottis is visible and notes that some patients require cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Most patients with severe enough obstruction to cause respiratory distress will not be able to be intubated with direct laryngoscopy or video-assisted indirect laryngoscopy.

canonical_statement: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rare progression of odontogenic infection and requires rapid airway assessment and surgical debridement.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Rarely, odontogenic infections can progress to necrotizing soft tissue infections such as necrotizing fasciitis. As with any anatomic site, this is a true surgical emergency, and rapid airway assessment and surgical debridement should be performed.

canonical_statement: The review identifies proper dental hygiene as the main preventive strategy and recommends regular brushing, flossing, and twice-yearly dental visits.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The mainstay of the prevention of odontogenic and orofacial infections is proper dental hygiene.

canonical_statement: Poor dental habits discussed by the review include highly acidic or sweet foods, tobacco, alcohol, and tooth grinding.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: These include consumption of highly acidic or sweet foods, consumption of tobacco products, consumption of alcohol, and tooth grinding

canonical_statement: Many odontogenic infections can be evaluated and managed at the bedside by clinical examination, with POCUS useful when the examination is equivocal.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Odontogenic infections can often be evaluated and managed at the bedside with a clinical exam alone. Many equivocal exams can be further clarified using POCUS

canonical_statement: The review cautions that contrast CT is often unnecessary and can add radiation, contrast-related risk, and incidental findings that trigger costly workup.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: CT scan with contrast is often not indicated and can expose patients to unnecessary neck radiation, risk contrast-associated complications, and unveil incidental findings that prompt unnecessary, costly workup.

canonical_statement: The review states that interprofessional collaboration among emergency, urgent-care, primary-care, dental, surgical, and otolaryngology clinicians can improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce patient harm.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Close collaboration with the emergency department, urgent care, and primary care providers, operating as an interprofessional team, can improve diagnostic accuracy and minimize physical and financial harm to the patient.

canonical_statement: The figure demonstrates marked submandibular swelling in a patient with Ludwig angina that limited assessment of neck extension.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Submandibular Swelling. Swelling in the submandibular area in a patient with Ludwig angina significantly limited the ability to assess neck extension.
